1.pericope_label: And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee. And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me.

schools.summary: Ellicott declines to name the speaker but reasons that the unexplained He could be none other than the Most High, marks the voice as articulate where the vision was not, explains the title as an idiom of the country the prophet lived in, and warns that no physical force is to be imagined, all of it still taking place within the vision.

Gill points back to the glorious Person on the throne and rules the spirit to be the Holy Spirit, the same that was in the living creatures and the wheels; Calvin reads the raising as a doctrine about two kinds of fear and then makes the order of voice and Spirit the lesson, since the efficacy of the word is not in the words themselves.

Clarke takes the spirit for a different one from that which moved the wheels, the spirit of prophecy whose office is to purify the heart, reads the standing as service before a master, and objects to the chapter division itself; Wesley names the speaker as Christ, counts the title ninety-five times at least, and puts the spirit with the one that actuated the living creatures.

Henry takes the title as a humble diminishing title, lest the man be lifted up with the abundance of the revelations, and marks that God passed by a retinue of angels ready to go on his errands to pitch on a son of man, the treasure being in earthen vessels.

debates.question: What is the spirit that entered him?

positions.position: The Holy Spirit, and the same Spirit that was in the living creatures and in the wheels.
A different spirit from the one that moved the wheels: the spirit of prophecy, whose office is to purify and refine the heart.
The Spirit of God, and no mere human vigour of the man's own.

debates.question: Why is he addressed as son of man?

positions.position: As a humble diminishing title, lest he be lifted up with the abundance of the revelations.
As an idiom of the country: the phrase is ordinary for man in the Aramaic tongues, and the prophet of the captivity was addressed in the common speech of the place he lived in.
The glorious Person on the throne described in the vision before.
Christ.
Unnamed, but in connection with that vision none other than the Most High.

outliers.claim: Objects to the chapter division itself: either the preceding chapter should have ended a verse earlier, or this verse belongs to it and the next should open the chapter.

Makes the sequence of voice and Spirit the lesson: nothing was accomplished by the voice until the Spirit was added, since the efficacy is not contained in the words themselves but proceeds from the secret instinct of the Spirit.

themes: And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee.
And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me.

3.pericope_label: And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day. For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God. And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them.

schools.summary: Ellicott settles who is meant by Israel after the captivity of the ten tribes, turns the word rendered nation against them as the term commonly used for the heathen, notes the pointing of the divine name, and divides the effect of the word rather than its outcome, a savour of death to one and of life to another.

Gill glosses hardness of face as we say a man is brazen faced, a forehead refusing to be ashamed and sin declared openly; Calvin sets face beside heart and finds an impiety too desperate for disguise, makes fruitless labour a rule against despondency, and closes on sign and word, since figures are illusory without an explanation.

Clarke traces the title through three stages, from this prophet to the other who saw visions in exile and then to the Man Christ Jesus, keeps the address concrete to those in captivity, and turns the messenger formula into a warning to preachers about their own creeds.

debates.question: What does the description of the hearers carry?

positions.position: Literally rebellious nations, the word being the one commonly used for the heathen, so that Israel is called rebellious heathen.
Hardness of face as well as of heart: an impiety so desperate that they opposed God without disguise, like horned oxen or furious bulls.
A brazen face, a forehead refusing to be ashamed, sin declared openly and not hidden.

debates.question: Why send a prophet to those who may not hear?

positions.position: So that he may not be discouraged beforehand if the ministry proves fruitless.
So that they may be assured God gave due warning and that they are inexcusable for not taking it.
To remove every pretext for error, God having another object in view besides the salvation of men.
Because the word cannot return void, though the character of its effect depends on those it comes to.

debates.question: Who are the children of Israel here?

positions.position: The two tribes with such others as had joined them, the continuity of the nation reckoned preserved in the remnant.
Those now in captivity in Chaldea particularly, and the Jews in general, far and near.

outliers.claim: Turns the messenger formula into a warning to preachers: let none suppose that because a thing agrees with his own creed it is therefore God's word, but bring the creed to the word first and try whether it is right.

Makes the vision depend on the voice: figures are illusory without an explanation, and signs presented to the eyes alone are dead images until the word throws life into them, which he applies to the sacraments.

themes: And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day.
For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God.
And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them.

6.pericope_label: And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns be with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house. And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious.

schools.summary: Ellicott settles the two words before anyone uses them: they occur nowhere else, the first might admit the marginal rendering rebels, but both should be taken together and as nouns rather than adjectives, which agrees with the scorpions that follow and with the strongly figurative manner of the book.

Gill takes the fear to be of the greatest among them, princes and nobles whose grandeur and stern looks and big words might awe a man; Calvin refuses to read the words as mere threats, takes them for the calumnies of men who claim the name of the Church, and holds that none are fit for the office but those armed with fortitude.

Clarke keeps the charge short, that they will maltreat him for the message but he must not suppress it; Wesley makes the words accusations and threats, reads the briers as running up among thorns, and closes with a sentence taken over almost verbatim from Henry.

Henry works the figure hard, briers and thorns as the fruit of sin and the curse and the scorpion's sting as a thousand times worse than a brier's scratch, adds that the man dwells among them and so is not safe in his own house, and observes that they were now in subjection and had only looks and words left them.

debates.question: What are the briers and thorns?

positions.position: Words occurring nowhere else, to be taken as nouns rather than adjectives, agreeing with the scorpions that follow.
The fruit of sin and the curse, of equal date with the enmity between the two seeds, hurtful to the ground and choking the good seed.
Briers running up among thorns, a fit emblem of the frowardness of sinners.

debates.question: What are the words that are not to be feared?

positions.position: Accusations, threats, or whatever a malicious heart can suggest to the tongue.
Not threats simply but calumnies, the boasts of men who take upon themselves the name of God and of the Church.
Big words backed by the grandeur and authority of princes and nobles.

debates.question: How far could their hostility go?

positions.position: No further than looks and words, since they were now themselves in subjection and divested of all power.
To real maltreatment for the message, which is no reason to suppress it.
To calumny that breaks the spirit, which is why none are fit for the office but those armed with fortitude.

outliers.claim: Sharpens the charge by where the man lives: he had been conversing with angels in vision, and coming down from that mount he finds he dwells among scorpions, as the Lord noticed of one of the churches that it dwelt where Satan's seat is.
Closes with a sentence taken over almost verbatim from Henry, that they who will do anything to purpose in the service of God must not fear the faces of men.

themes: And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns be with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house.
And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious.

8.pericope_label: But thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house: open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee. And when I looked, behold, an hand was sent unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein; And he spread it before me; and it was written within and without: and there was written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe.

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the eating inside the vision, corrects the hand from was sent to was put forth and makes it a cherub's or one from the throne, explains how a roll was read with one hand unrolling and the other winding up, takes the writing on both sides for the fullness of the message, and bounds the mournful character to the years before the judgment fell.

Gill makes the hand Christ's own and the likeness of a hand rather than a real one, and draws the order of ministry from the hearing that precedes speaking; Calvin finds in the visible hand the certainty a bare volume would have lacked, gives the etymology of the roll, and hears in the three words a length of time imposed rather than a brief errand.

Clarke makes the eating dietary and the hand an emblem of divine power, testifies to the ordinary one-sided roll from his own collection, and sets the letter that killeth against the mercy of glad tidings; Wesley describes the parchment fastened piece to piece and wrapped about a rod, and notes the writing on both the inward and the outward side.

debates.question: Whose hand held out the roll?

positions.position: Not an angel's but Christ's own, and the likeness of a hand rather than a real one.
A hand stretched out to him, either a cherub's or one from the throne above.
An emblem of divine power, the owner left unnamed.

debates.question: Why was the roll written on both sides?

positions.position: To denote the fullness of the message, rolls being ordinarily written on one side only.
Because the prophecy was long and all to one effect, so that they might see the mind of God wherever they looked.

debates.question: How far does the mournful character of the message extend?

positions.position: Over the whole of it and over much time: not sweet but full of sorrow, the man a herald denouncing war with no message of peace.
Only until the judgment fell, after which the prophecies turn consolatory.
It is the letter that killeth, to be set against the mercy of glad tidings.

outliers.claim: Testifies from his own shelves: several Hebrew rolls written on the inside only, a Sanskrit roll of sixty feet also written only within, and a Koran two inches broad and twelve feet long weighing half an ounce.
Names the stumbling-block the charge removes: a multitude has great power to disturb us, the consent of a whole people being a tempest in which even those not wicked are carried along.

themes: But thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house: open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee.
And when I looked, behold, an hand was sent unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein;
And he spread it before me; and it was written within and without: and there was written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe.
